hops.afterHeading: The problem: a rough first draft
hops.title: The temporary inner-ear organ that triggers bursts before hearing
hops.text: Before a newborn rat hears a single sound, its cochlea is already busy. A temporary ridge of supporting cells called Kölliker's organ releases puffs of ATP on its own. This ATP release can trigger potassium release from the supporting cells, depolarizing neighbouring inner hair cells so they release glutamate, and can drive coordinated bursts in nearby auditory nerve fibres without sound. That may help the brain sharpen its pitch map. Around the time rats begin responding to airborne sound, Kölliker's organ regresses as the inner sulcus takes shape, and the ATP-driven bursts fade. In humans it has already disappeared by birth.

hops.afterHeading: Why activity? Two neighbours look the same to a gradient
hops.title: Sleep twitches are not just dreams of chasing rabbits
hops.text: When a sleeping puppy jerks a paw, people assume it is chasing rabbits in a dream. The biologist George Romanes made the same guess about sleeping ferrets in 1883. But infant rats and adult cats keep twitching even when the cerebral cortex is disconnected from the brainstem, so those animals can twitch without a signal from the cortex. In newborn rats, brief twitches occur against a background of muscle atonia and can cluster across limbs; feedback from a twitch can trigger a burst in the matching patch of sensory cortex: forelimb to forelimb area, hindlimb to hindlimb area. Matched timing may help wire the body map.

sources.citation: Blumberg MS. Front Neurol 1:140 (2010). PMCID PMC3034236.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A sleeping puppy curled on a woven rug with one front paw lifting in a small twitch while its body stays relaxed.
image.caption: In infant rats, sleep twitches start below the cortex and send feedback that may help wire the body map.

hops.afterHeading: Disrupt the correlation, keep plenty of spikes
hops.title: Goldfish that regrew their optic nerves under a strobe light
hops.text: If uncorrelated spikes leave a map blurry, what happens when every ganglion cell fires in lockstep? In 1985, John Schmidt and Leslie Eisele let goldfish regrow a cut optic nerve in a featureless tank lit only by a flashing xenon strobe. Each flash drove neighbouring and distant cells at nearly the same instant. Spikes kept arriving, yet sites in the midbrain target responded to patches averaging 32 degrees across, compared with 11 to 12 degrees in fish that regrew the nerve under normal light. Returning the fish to normal light after day 35 barely sharpened them. When everyone fires at once, timing cannot tell neighbours from strangers.

sources.citation: Schmidt JT, Eisele LE. Neuroscience 14(2):535–546 (1985). PMID 2986040.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An orange goldfish swimming in a bare glass aquarium under a bright flashing overhead strobe lamp in a dark room.
image.caption: Under a strobe, midbrain sites in regrowing goldfish answered to patches averaging 32 degrees, nearly three times the normal-light average.
